**Verified working.** A dedicated verification driver (`/tmp/diag_timerfix`, dumping `iop_timers_get_state()`'s full 6-channel array at the end of the same boot trace) confirms `t[5].mode = 0x00000C70` - the low byte genuinely reflects the real `0x70` write (bits 4-6, `IOP_CNT_MODE_TARGET_INTR`/`OVERFL_INTR`/`ZERO_RETURN` per `iop_timers.h`'s bit layout) that was previously silently dropped into plain RAM instead of reaching the timer model at all. `t[5].target = 0x00012000` is also genuinely nonzero (written via the pre-existing, already-correct 32-bit path), and `t[5].count = 0x07B87803` shows the timer has been actively ticking - all consistent with a real, functioning periodic timer configuration that this project's model can now actually see, where before this fix it could not.

**`iop_icfg`: inconclusive - the address was never touched in this trace window.** `0x1F801450` did not appear anywhere in the width tally at all (0 accesses of any width - 8, 16, or 32) across the full 44-second run. This means the current boot path (still reaching its familiar `idle=1` steady state, task #238) simply never executes the real BIOS code that would write ICFG within this trace's budget - not that 16-bit access definitely doesn't happen, nor that it definitely does. Per this project's own established discipline (task #180's lesson, restated in the 114th/115th findings: never fabricate behavior for real, BIOS-resident internal bookkeeping without live evidence), no change was made to `iop_icfg.c` or its dispatch. Task #244 is left open, re-scoped as "no evidence either way yet - revisit if/when a future round's boot progress reaches whatever real code path touches this register."

**Verification**: full regression suite re-run clean, 90/90 pass, 0 failures. Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild (`make clean && make`, exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.dol`/`.elf` produced; same one pre-existing, harmless `-Wstringop-truncation` warning in `locate_and_parse_romdir`, unrelated to this round's change).

## 116th finding (Round 76, task #221/#245, task #172 continuation): device-table panic loop mechanically re-disassembled with Capstone - it is a deliberate "should-never-return" trap, not an unconditional dead-end; the 92nd finding's framing was imprecise

Per the user's explicit "fix the prid" direction, this round resumed task #221 (deprioritized at the 93rd finding) with better tooling than previous rounds had available (Capstone MIPS disassembler, not ad hoc byte-level reading), disassembling the real ROM functions the 92nd finding had identified but never actually decoded: `0xBFC4A600`, `0xBFC4A7F0`, `0xBFC4A9FC` (the case-4 handler `0xBFC4A7F0` dispatches to), and `0xBFC4AED0`. No source change made - docs-only investigation round, regression/rebuild skipped per standing convention.

**`0xBFC4AED0` is a generic I-cache flush utility, not device-specific logic.** Full disassembly shows: save COP0 Status, save/clear `ICFG` (`0x1F801450`) and an adjacent unnamed register (`0x1F801578`), save the real R3000A cache-control register (physical `0xFFFE0130`, the well-known "BIU/cache config" register on this CPU), isolate the cache (`Status.IsC=1`), zero 0xF80 bytes of cache-line-aligned data (the standard real I-cache invalidation idiom), then restore everything in reverse order and return. This is boilerplate called unconditionally between processing each device-table slot - it was never part of the "device driver" logic the 92nd finding was trying to attribute it to.

**`0xBFC4A600` validates and parses one raw device-table entry into a 9-word header struct** (magic-number checks at offsets 0/0x14, a length-under-0x20 check at offset 2, a masked-field check at offset 0x10, then a classification value returned in `$v0` based on further field comparisons at offsets 2/0x14/8 relative to the ORIGINAL entry). Offset 4 of the OUTPUT struct is populated from the raw entry's offset `0x10` - this is the field that later gets used as a real function pointer.

**`0xBFC4A7F0` is a real device-type dispatcher, not a panic path.** Branches on a type field (`0`,`1`,`3`,`4` are the only handled/recognized values - anything else, including `2` and any value `>4`, returns `v0=-1` "unsupported type" and is NOT fatal); types `1`/`3`/`4` each call a distinct sub-handler (`0xBFC4A918`/`0xBFC4A998`/`0xBFC4A9FC` respectively) then converge on a SHARED struct-populate helper and return `v0=0` normally. This directly disproves the 92nd finding's characterization of this function as leading to an "unconditional" dead end - it has entirely normal, non-fatal return paths for every input.

**The real, precise mechanics of the panic loop** (`0xBFC4A454-0xBFC4A464`, re-confirmed unchanged from the 92nd finding's disassembly, `sb $v0,(0x80000000)` then an unconditional `j` to itself): tracing the caller (`0xBFC4A280-0xBFC4A488`, the function orchestrating both device-table slots) shows it processes device slot 1 (`0xBFC4A330-0xBFC4A3A4`: classify via `0xBFC4A600`, dispatch via `0xBFC4A7F0`, flush cache via `0xBFC4AED0`, then call a REAL function pointer loaded from the parsed struct's offset 4 - `sp+0x14` for slot 1) and observes it return normally (execution continues into slot 2's processing at `0xBFC4A3A8`). Slot 2 goes through the identical classify/dispatch/flush sequence, then calls ITS OWN parsed function pointer (`sp+0x3c`) at `0xBFC4A44C` - and falls STRAIGHT into the `0x80000000`-write-and-loop trap immediately afterward, with no other check in between. **This is not an accident or an unconditional wall - it is a deliberate real-hardware safety trap for exactly one specific case: slot 2's real function pointer is architecturally expected to NEVER return** (almost certainly a genuine kernel/OS hand-off - real retail PS2 IOP BIOS boot sequences end by permanently transferring control, similar in spirit to `_ExecPS2`/`ExecKernel`-style hand-offs already documented elsewhere in this project's SIF/RPC investigation threads). Slot 1's function pointer, by contrast, is fully expected to return (that's how slot 2 gets reached at all).

**Honest reframing of task #221.** The real, concrete open question is no longer "what do these mystery functions do" (now mechanically understood via static disassembly) but specifically: **what real function does slot 2's data-dependent function pointer actually resolve to, and why would it return in this project's emulation instead of taking over permanently as real hardware does.** Answering this requires LIVE tracing with `PRId=0x1f` temporarily re-enabled in a disposable scratch copy (never committed) - reading the actual raw device-table bytes at the `$a0`/`$s2` pointers this round's static disassembly could only describe structurally, and logging the real resolved jalr target at `0xBFC4A44C`. This is a legitimate next step, not deprioritized guesswork, but was not completed this round given the depth already reached - flagged as the concrete continuation for task #245.

**No fix applied.** Per this project's own established discipline (never fabricate real, BIOS-resident internal bookkeeping without live evidence - most recently restated in the 114th/115th findings), no source change was made pending the live trace described above. `PRId` remains at its existing safe value of 0.

## 117th finding (Round 77, task #221/#245, task #172 continuation): device-table entries are genuine embedded IOP IRX/ELF modules - implemented a real intercept reusing the existing ELF loader; escapes the literal panic loop for the first time, but reveals a deeper, not-yet-modeled dependency

Directly continuing the 116th finding's concrete next step (live-trace the real device-table bytes). Per the user's "lets go" direction, this round went further than tracing alone: implemented and tested a real fix, with full honesty about what it does and doesn't yet solve.

**The raw device-table "entries" are literal ELF32/MIPS headers.** Dumping the raw bytes at both slots' pointers (`0xBFC1E830` for slot 1, `0xBFC1FA50` for slot 2 - captured via a live JAL-argument-watching hook on `0xBFC4A600`) shows the real ELF magic (`7F 45 4C 46`), `e_machine=8` (EM_MIPS), and a vendor `e_type=0xFF80` - **exactly** the real, cited "Sony IOP IRX" format `source/hw/iop_elf.c` already fully supports (see that file's own extensive citation header, task #92). Both entries' single `PT_LOAD` program header (type 1) has `p_vaddr=p_paddr=0`, confirming these images are meant to be relocated to a real load address chosen at boot time - not run in place. This means the "device table" this project's 92nd/93rd/116th findings treated as a mysterious, custom structure is actually **two more real IOP IRX modules**, discovered via a different ROM entry path (a config-string-driven table) than the ROMDIR list `iop_module_loader.c` already parses, but in the identical binary format.

**Corrected field-tracing error from the 116th finding.** Re-disassembling `0xBFC4A600` with the correct base register (`$a2 = $t0+0x14`, not `$t0` directly, as the 116th finding's write-up mistakenly implied) shows the classifier copies several ELF-header-relative fields into an output struct, including the real `e_entry` (`*(t0+0x18)`) at output offset 0x10 and `e_phoff`/`e_shoff` at 0x14/0x18 - but the field the caller ultimately treats as a callable function pointer is populated later, by `0xBFC4A7F0`'s type-specific sub-handlers (`0xBFC4A918`/`0xBFC4A998`/`0xBFC4A9FC`), not directly by the classifier. Live tracing confirmed the real ROM code calls this field as-is, unrelocated: `jalr 0x00000890` for slot 1, `jalr 0x00000030` for slot 2 - both far too small to be any real code address this project has ever loaded a module at, consistent with "raw/unrelocated ELF header field, never actually run through a loader."

**Fix implemented** (`source/core/iop/iop_core.c`): the JAL case now remembers the raw device-table image pointer whenever the real ROM calls `0xBFC4A600` (only when `cop0[15]==0x1f` - completely inert, zero behavior change, at the shipped default `PRId=0`, since this ROM code path is never even reached then). The JALR case, at the two exact real call sites (`0xBFC4A39C` for slot 1, `0xBFC4A44C` for slot 2), now calls the existing, already-tested `iop_elf_load()` (the same function `iop_module_loader.c` uses for every ROMDIR module) on the remembered raw image, at fixed load addresses (`0x001C0000`/`0x001C8000`) chosen with a wide safety margin from both the ROMDIR loader's own bump-allocated region (measured peak `0x00145CA0` across a full 29-module boot) and the stack (`0x001FFF00`), then redirects the jump to the real, correctly-relocated entry point instead of the raw header field. On any load failure, falls back to the ROM's own value - a safe degrade, never worse than today.

**Verified this changes behavior - a real, if partial, step forward.** Live host-native tracing (scratch copy, `PRId` temporarily forced to `0x1f`, never committed that way) shows the IOP genuinely no longer gets stuck at the exact literal panic-loop PC (`0xBFC4A458`) - for the first time in this entire multi-round investigation thread. Instead, it now executes real, freshly-ELF-loaded code that eventually settles into a NEW spin pattern at very low RAM addresses (observed PC slowly advancing through `0x00000050-0x00000090` over 108 million executed instructions in a 40-second trace - i.e., genuinely running, not crashed, but making almost no forward progress).

**Honest assessment - this is not yet a working boot path.** The new low-address spin strongly suggests the freshly-loaded device module's own real init code depends on some further real, low-RAM boot infrastructure (exception-vector tables, `boot_info`-style structures - similar in spirit to `iop_excb.c`'s already-modeled `RAM[0x100]` chain, task #22/#134) that never gets set up on the `PRId=0x1f` path, because `iop_module_loader_boot()` (which sets up equivalent scaffolding for the ROMDIR path) never triggers here either (per the well-established citation already in `iop_core.c`: it only activates when real ROM code's PC escapes into memory this project doesn't model, which doesn't happen on the corrected-PRId path). This confirms the Round 59/60 caution was well-founded: enabling `PRId=0x1f` bypasses a large amount of scaffolding this project's fallback system currently provides, and one more ELF-loader fix is not sufficient to replace all of it. **`PRId` remains at its safe value of 0 in the shipped default build - this fix is verified inert there (full 90/90 regression pass, clean Wii rebuild) and only changes behavior in the not-yet-enabled `PRId=0x1f` configuration.**

**Concrete next step for task #245**: identify what real low-RAM structure the freshly-loaded module's code is spinning on around `0x50-0x90` (likely by disassembling the ELF-loaded image's own code at its real relocated address this time, now that it's genuinely loaded and traceable, rather than the raw ROM bytes) and determine whether it's a real dependency this project needs to model, or a symptom of an incomplete/wrong relocation in this round's intercept itself.

**Verification**: full regression suite re-run clean, 90/90 pass, 0 failures. Clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild (`make clean && make`, exit 0, `pcsx2-wii-git.dol`/`.elf` produced; same one pre-existing, harmless `-Wstringop-truncation` warning, unrelated to this round's change).

## 118th finding (Round 78, task #245, task #172 continuation): the PRId=0x1f spin isolated to an exact 11-instruction self-loop in a real, pre-existing low-RAM kernel stub - unrelated to the 117th finding's ELF-load fix, and predates it

Directly continuing the 117th finding's own flagged next step (identify what the freshly-loaded module's code is spinning on). This round isolated the spin to an exact instruction sequence and, importantly, ruled out the 117th finding's own fix as the cause.

**The spin is a precise, 11-instruction self-loop, not a wide/vague hang.** A full PC-histogram of the entire 40-second, 108-million-instruction trace (scratch copy, `PRId` temporarily forced to `0x1f`, never committed) shows exactly 11 addresses (`0x54, 0x58, 0x5C, 0x60, 0x64, 0x68, 0x6C, 0x80, 0x84, 0x88, 0x8C`) each hit ~3.62 million times - three orders of magnitude more than anything else in the entire run (the next-busiest address, part of the freshly-ELF-loaded slot 2 module, is hit only ~4,900 times). Every other address this function's own prologue occupies (`0x34-0x50`) was hit exactly **once** - the function's setup code runs a single time, then execution never leaves the tail 11 instructions again.

**Root cause of the self-loop, mechanically confirmed.** Disassembling this exact span: the function saves `$ra` to the stack in its prologue (`sw $ra, 0x18($sp)` at `0x38`) but its epilogue (`jr $ra` at `0x88`) never restores it - there is no `lw $ra, 0x18($sp)` anywhere in the observed path back to that `jr`. Because the function's own body issues two internal `jal`s before reaching the loop tail (`jal 0x33c` at `0x3C`, `jal 0x318` at `0x4C`), and the second one (`jal 0x318`) sets `$ra` to `0x54` (the instruction right after its own delay slot) as a side effect of the `jal` instruction itself - and nothing between `0x54` and the final `jr $ra` at `0x88` issues another `jal`/`jalr` to overwrite it again - `$ra` is still `0x54` when `jr $ra` executes. The result: the function returns "to itself," re-entering at `0x54` forever, regenerating the exact same 11-instruction sequence indefinitely.

**Confirmed this is NOT caused by the 117th finding's ELF-load intercept.** This function lives at IOP RAM `0x30-0x90` - nowhere near either of the fixed load addresses that fix uses (`0x001C0000`/`0x001C8000`). A control run with the exact same real BIOS, but `PRId` left at its shipped default of `0` (where the 117th finding's intercept never triggers at all), shows **completely different data** at `0x30-0x90` - unrelated bytes, not this function. This proves the function is written into low RAM by some *earlier* real ROM boot step that only executes once `PRId=0x1f` unlocks the real boot path (matching this project's own long-standing citation that the real PRId diverts ROM code onto an entirely different, more complete boot sequence before it ever reaches the device-table logic the 116th/117th findings targeted) - not something introduced by this round's own fix.

**Honest assessment - two live hypotheses, not yet distinguished.** Either (a) this is a genuine bug in how this project's interpreter or memory model handles whatever real ROM step writes this stub into RAM (a dropped/mis-relocated instruction, since a real compiler would never omit an `$ra` restore after explicitly saving it), or (b) this is deliberate real hardware behavior - a classic embedded-kernel "default/idle handler" stub, intentionally self-looping until some future step overwrites this RAM region with the real handler or an interrupt-driven state change redirects execution - a pattern this project has resolved many times before for other "polling loop" boot walls (WaitSema, CreateSema, etc.) by identifying and implementing the real missing event. No fix was attempted this round, since distinguishing (a) from (b) needs further tracing (specifically: identifying which real ROM function writes this stub, and whether real hardware's compiled version of it truly omits the restore or whether this project's copy/relocation of it is dropping an instruction) rather than a guess.

**No source change this round** - docs-only investigation, regression/rebuild skipped per standing convention. `PRId` remains at its safe value of 0 in the shipped build.

**Concrete next step for task #245**: trace backward from where this stub gets written into RAM (search for the writing instruction(s) targeting `0x30-0x90`, likely a `sw`/`sb` sequence during an earlier real ROM function, well before the device-table code at `0xBFC4A2xx+`) to identify the real source function and cross-check its actual compiled form for the missing restore.

## 119th finding (Round 79, task #245, task #172 continuation): live real-hardware comparison (PCSX2 DebugServer + real, legally-dumped GT3) conclusively resolves the 118th finding - our PRId=0x1f low-RAM content is genuinely wrong, not a deliberate real idle stub

Per the user's direction to "boot GT3 up again," connected to a live, running PCSX2 instance (DebugServer, real GT3/SCES-50294 disc, the same reference environment used for the 55th finding) to check what real retail IOP hardware actually has at the exact RAM addresses where the 118th finding found this project's own PRId=0x1f trace stuck in a self-loop.

**Real hardware's actual code at these addresses, read live via `pcsx2_disassemble(cpu=iop)`:**
- `0x00-0x0C`: four `nop`s (the real UTLB-refill vector - IOP has no real TLB, matches this project's own existing "no TLB modeled" note).
- `0x10-0x3C`: twelve `break` instructions (unused padding/placeholder space).
- `0x40-0x74`: a genuine, clean exception-context-save routine - `sw k0/k1` of `EPC`/`Cause`/`Status`/`COP0 r7` into a fixed save area (`0x420-0x430`), then `li k1,0x3C; lw k1,0x440(k1); mtc0 zero,C0r7; jr k1` - a fixed-index (not Cause-derived) jump through a real, RAM-resident handler-pointer table.
- `0x80-0xB4`: **the real, canonical MIPS general-exception vector** (physical `0x80`, matching `Status.BEV=0`'s standard vector `0x80000080`) - and it is the textbook pattern: save `$at`/`$k0`/`EPC`/`Status`/`Cause` to a fixed area (`0x400-0x40C`), then `andi k0, Cause, 0x3C` (masking out the real `Cause.ExcCode` field, bits 2-5), `lw k0, 0x440(k0)` (indexing a genuine 16-entry, `Cause.ExcCode`-keyed jump table based at RAM `0x440`, spanning to `0x47C` - the same table base the `0x40` routine also reads from, just at a fixed index instead of a computed one), then `jr k0`. This is real, live, unambiguous confirmation of exactly the kind of "real RAM-resident exception dispatch table" this project's `iop_excb.c` (task #22/#134's `RAM[0x100]` table) already models the *concept* of, just for a genuinely different, more fundamental table (`RAM[0x440]`, the actual CPU-level MIPS exception vector table, not the higher-level LOADCORE registration list `iop_excb.c` targets).

**Compared directly against this project's own PRId=0x1f trace at the identical addresses** (the exact RAM dump already captured for the 118th finding): completely different content. Where real hardware has the clean save/dispatch routine above, this project's PRId=0x1f run has the 118th finding's mystery function (prologue at `0x34-0x50`, the missing-`$ra`-restore self-loop at `0x54-0x8C`) - and, critically, this now-confirmed real general-exception-vector address (`0x80-0xB4`) contains, in this project's run, more of that SAME mystery function's continuation (`nop, nop, jr $ra, addiu $sp,$sp,0x20` at `0x80-0x8C` - literally the self-loop's own tail, not anything resembling a context-save dispatcher).

**Conclusion: the 118th finding's two hypotheses are resolved.** This is not deliberate real "idle handler" design (hypothesis b) - it's confirmed, via direct comparison with live real hardware, that this project's `PRId=0x1f` boot path is not installing the real, universal exception-vector/dispatch-table structure into low IOP RAM at all (hypothesis a). Real hardware installs this structure extremely early - almost certainly before any of the device-table/module-specific logic the 116th/117th findings targeted - as one of the first things any real IOP kernel does at cold boot. This project's `PRId=0x1f` path evidently skips or mis-executes whatever real ROM step is responsible for this, leaving low RAM populated with unrelated, incidental content from elsewhere that this project's interpreter then mis-executes as if it were real code.

**Scope reframing for task #245.** This narrows the investigation meaningfully: the real blocker is no longer "what does this specific device-table entry's function do" (resolved, 116th/117th findings) but "why doesn't this project's `PRId=0x1f` boot path execute whatever real, universal ROM step installs the CPU-level exception-vector table at RAM `0x400-0x47C`+ before anything else runs." This is a more foundational question than the device-table mechanism itself, and answering it will likely require tracing much earlier in the `PRId=0x1f` boot sequence than the `0xBFC4A2xx+` region this thread has focused on so far.

**No fix attempted this round** - live comparison and documentation only. `PRId` remains at its safe value of 0 in the shipped build. No source change; regression/rebuild skipped per standing convention for docs-only rounds.

## 120th finding (Round 80, task #244/#245, task #172 continuation): real reset-vector PRId dispatch found and verified correct in this project's own emulator - conclusively closes task #244, and locates the next lead for task #245

Per the user's "yes" to continue tracing what real ROM function installs the exception-vector table, this round went back to the true beginning: the raw MIPS reset vector, `0xBFC00000` itself, via full static disassembly of `/tmp/real_bios.bin` (Capstone, targeted-window mode to avoid the linear disassembler's tendency to desync on non-code bytes).

**The real reset vector is a PRId-keyed two-way dispatch, not a single linear path.** `0xBFC00000-0xBFC0002C`: `mfc0 $k0, cop0r15` (PRId) immediately at reset, `slti $at, $k0, 0x59`, then branches to `0xBFC02000` if `PRId < 0x59`, or falls through to `0xBFC00800` if `PRId >= 0x59`. This is a real, hardware-level fork in the boot ROM keyed directly on the same COP0 register this entire investigation thread (91st finding onward) has centered on.

**Verified via host-native trace that this project's own emulator takes the CORRECT branch for its shipped `PRId=0`.** A disposable `DIAG_RESET_TRACE` hook (scratch copy `/tmp/pcsx2-instrument8`, never committed) logging every IOP `pc`/`cop0[15]` value from the very first step confirms: `pc` goes `0xBFC00000 -> ... -> 0xBFC00010 -> 0xBFC00024 -> ... -> 0xBFC00030 -> 0xBFC02000` - exactly the `PRId<0x59` branch, matching what real hardware would do for `PRId=0` (which is indeed `< 0x59`). This project's reset-vector interpretation is correct and needed no fix.

**This conclusively closes task #244 (iop_icfg 16-bit dispatch gap) as verified-correct, not "no evidence yet."** Continuing to disassemble the `0xBFC02000` path (the branch this project's `PRId=0` actually takes) reveals it repeatedly gates its own IOP_ICFG (`0x1F801450`, read via `0xBF801450`) checks behind an earlier `PRId<0x10` test - seen twice, at `0xBFC02028-0xBFC0203C` and again at `0xBFC02368-0xBFC02380` - both structured as `mfc0 $t0,cop0r15; slti $at,$t0,0x10; bnez $at,<skip>; <only then read ICFG>`. Since this project's shipped `PRId=0` satisfies `PRId<0x10`, BOTH of these checks take the early branch and skip the ICFG read entirely - real, structural, ROM-level behavior, not a gap in this project's own MMIO dispatch. Task #244's original "no access observed in the 44s trace window" finding is now fully explained and closed: real hardware, at this exact `PRId` value, never touches `IOP_ICFG` this early either.

**The `0xBFC02000` routine is genuine low-level hardware bring-up, not yet the vector-table content itself.** Beyond the ICFG checks, this function: sets the boot-progress byte at `0xBF802070` incrementally (values 1 through 9+, a real ROM convention for early POST-style progress reporting), zeroes IOP RAM `0x000-0xF80` in two passes (a sparse 8-word/block pass, then a full 32-word/block pass - covering, notably, the exact `0x400-0x47C` region the 119th finding identified as the real vector-table's eventual location, but only clearing it here, not yet populating it), writes the real IOP cache-control register (`0xFFFE0130`), and performs several cache-line touch/warm reads from `0xA0000000`. This matches the profile of genuine early POST/hardware-init code, consistent with (not contradicting) the 119th finding's framing that the actual vector-table *content* install happens as a distinct, later step.

**Found the likely next link in the chain: a repeated loader-call pattern structurally identical to the 117th finding's device-table mechanism.** At `0xBFC023D0` and `0xBFC0242C`, the ROM calls a common subroutine at `0xBFC02600` with `$a0`/`$a1` set to two different ROM banks (`0xBFC0xxxx` and `0xBFC8xxxx`) and `$a2` pointing at small table entries (`0xBFC02478`/`0xBFC02488`/`0xBFC02498`/`0xBFC024A0`) - then, exactly like the already-documented `0xBFC4A600`/`0xBFC4A7F0` device-table mechanism, conditionally `jr $v0` into whatever entry point the call returns, passing a flag byte read from the same table entry as `$a0`. This is a strong structural match for "load/verify a ROM-embedded image, get back an entry point, jump into it if valid" - the same shape as the already-solved device-table loader, but earlier in boot and operating on different table entries and ROM banks. This subroutine (`0xBFC02600`) has not yet been disassembled.

**No fix this round - static analysis and closure only.** Task #244 closed. Task #245's concrete next step: disassemble `0xBFC02600` and the table entries feeding it (`0xBFC02478-0xBFC024A8`) to determine whether this is (or leads to) the real vector-table installer the 119th finding showed is missing from this project's `PRId=0x1f` path. `PRId` remains at its safe value of 0 in the shipped build; no source change, regression/rebuild skipped per standing convention for docs-only rounds.

## 121st finding (Round 81, task #245, task #172 continuation): 0xBFC02600 is a real ROMDIR-catalog scanner (RAM_SIZE config + optional-bank bootstrap), confirmed to succeed in this project's own trace, and its escape hatch lands directly in the already-documented device-table investigation neighborhood - closing the gap between the reset vector and the 116th-120th findings' thread

Directly continuing the 120th finding's flagged next step (disassemble `0xBFC02600` and its feeding table entries).

**`0xBFC02600` is a linear ROMDIR-catalog scan, not an image loader.** Disassembly shows it walks a table from `$a0` to `$a1` in 0x10-byte strides, comparing each entry's 8-byte name field and a size field against a caller-supplied criteria block (`$a2`), accumulating a running offset (`$t2`) as it skips non-matching entries. On a match, it returns the accumulated address in `$v0`; on reaching `$a1` with no match, returns `0`.

**The catalog it scans is a real, standard PS2 IOP ROMDIR.** The data table at `0xBFC02700` onward contains, in order, the exact real IOP kernel module name strings: `RESET`, `ROMDIR`, `EXTINFO`, `SBIN`, `LOGO`, `IOPBTCONF` (twice), `SYSMEM`, `LOADCORE`, `EXCEPMAN`, `SIFMAN`, `SIFCMD`, `INTRMAN`, and more following the identical stride/format this project's own `iop_module_loader.c` (task #92/#33) already parses - just a separate instance of the format, read here for a different, earlier purpose (real hardware evidently keeps more than one ROMDIR-shaped table in ROM).

**The caller uses this scan to configure real memory-size hardware and optionally boot an alternate ROM-bank image.** Before calling `0xBFC02600`, the caller reads a size field from the matched entry and writes it to `0xBF801060` - the real, well-known PS1/PS2 IOP `RAM_SIZE` configuration register. If the scan finds a match, the caller `jr $v0`s into the returned address (passing a flag byte as `$a0`) - i.e., an optional "alternate/expansion ROM image" bootstrap, tried once for the `0xBFC0xxxx` bank and once for `0xBFC8xxxx`.

**If neither bank yields a match, this is a real, deliberate fatal trap** (`0xBFC02454-0xBFC02470`: sets the boot-progress byte to `0xFA`, then an unconditional `b` back to itself forever) - structurally the same kind of real-hardware safety trap already documented for the device-table mechanism's slot-2 dead end (116th finding), just for a different real failure condition (no valid ROMDIR catalog found in either bank - should never happen on real, well-formed retail hardware).

**Verified via host-native trace that this project's own execution takes the successful path, matching real hardware.** A second disposable hook (`DIAG_FATAL_LOOP`, scratch copy, never committed) counting hits on the fatal-trap addresses across a 2,000,000-step run shows zero hits at `0xBFC02454`/`0xBFC02460`/`0xBFC0246C` - the catalog scan succeeds (as it must, since this is a real, valid retail BIOS dump) and execution escapes the `0xBFC02000-0xBFC02710` region entirely by the 51st IOP step.

**The escape lands at `0xBFC4B800`** - directly adjacent to, and clearly part of the same real kernel-bootstrap neighborhood as, the already-extensively-documented device-table mechanism (`0xBFC4A600`/`0xBFC4A7F0`, 116th-119th findings). This closes a real gap in this investigation thread: the raw reset vector (`0xBFC00000`, 120th finding) now has a fully-traced, unbroken static path all the way to the device-table logic this project already understands in detail - via PRId dispatch -> RAM/cache bring-up -> ROMDIR catalog scan/RAM_SIZE config -> `0xBFC4B800`. The run continues healthily far beyond this in our own trace (reaching real IOP RAM execution around `0x001A44F8` by 2,000,000 steps), consistent with the project's already-documented, working default-`PRId=0` boot progress.

**Reframing for task #245 - and a self-correction caught before it was recorded wrong.** The real exception-vector-table install (119th finding: RAM `0x400-0x47C`) has still not been directly located. It is not in any of the code traced so far (reset vector, `0xBFC02000`'s bring-up, or the `0xBFC02600` catalog scanner) - all of which this project's own emulator already executes correctly and without incident, per this round's and the 120th finding's clean host traces. An initial draft of this finding proposed the still-unexamined `0xBFC00800` branch (`PRId>=0x59`) as the next step, reasoning that the install must live on "the one branch not yet followed." Re-checking this project's own already-established real PRId value before finalizing - the 91st finding cites real PCSX2's `psxReset()` setting `PRid=0x0000001f` verbatim, the same value this project's own inert `PRId=0x1f` gates use throughout tasks #245/#221 - shows `0x1f < 0x59`. **Real PS2 hardware itself takes the exact same `0xBFC02000` branch this project's default `PRId=0` build already takes**, not the `0xBFC00800` branch. The `0xBFC00800` path is therefore very unlikely to be where the real install lives (it may only ever run in non-retail/development-unit configurations with a different PRId) and is not a productive next step. The real install must instead be reached inside `0xBFC4B800` (this round's escape point, not yet disassembled) or somewhere further along the SAME `0xBFC02000`-rooted path this project's own emulator already walks correctly.

**No fix this round - static analysis and host-native verification only.** `PRId` remains at its safe value of 0 in the shipped build; no source change, regression/rebuild skipped per standing convention for docs-only rounds.

**Concrete next step for task #245**: disassemble `0xBFC4B800` (the real code this project's own successful catalog-scan escape lands in) - not `0xBFC00800`, which real retail hardware's own established PRId (`0x1f`) never even reaches, per the self-correction above.

## 122nd finding (Round 82, task #245, task #172 continuation): located and verified the real IOP kernel-main init dispatcher (0xBFC5289C) and mapped its ~30-subroutine call graph - the exact vector-table install site is still not pinpointed, and a naive static search rules out the simplest possible mechanism

Directly continuing the 121st finding's flagged next step (disassemble `0xBFC4B800`).

**`0xBFC4B800` is a second-stage bootstrap, not the kernel proper.** It clears the real IOP kernel's BSS-style scratch region (`0x80007ffc` downward), sets up a fresh kernel stack (`$sp` derived from `$a0<<0x14 + 0x80000000 - 0x100`), stores three early boot-parameter scalars into RAM `0x60`/`0x64`/`0x68`, then unconditionally `j`s (no return) to `0xBFC5289C`. A structurally-similar PRId-dispatch fork (identical in shape to the reset vector's own `PRId<0x59` check, 120th finding) sits immediately afterward at `0xBFC4B900` in ROM layout, but a host-native trace (`DIAG_FATAL_LOOP` hook extended to also count hits on `0xBFC4B900`, scratch copy, never committed) shows **zero hits** there across a 2,000,000-step run - it is not part of this execution path, just adjacent code, and this round is careful not to claim otherwise.

**`0xBFC5289C` is confirmed, via host trace, to be the real kernel-main init dispatcher.** The same extended hook shows `0xBFC4B800` hit exactly once (IOP step 7,941) and `0xBFC5289C` hit exactly once (IOP step 20,228) - both reached, in the right order, exactly as this round's static reading of the code predicted. This is real, further-confirmed forward progress along the chain from the raw reset vector (120th finding) through the ROMDIR-catalog scanner (121st finding) to this point.

**The function's body is a real subsystem-by-subsystem kernel bring-up sequence**, matching the classic shape of a ps2sdk-style `_start()`: repeated SPU2 per-voice register mutes (`0x1F801C00`+, zeroing offsets `0x180`-`0x186`), a real DMA-channel clear (`0x1F801070`+, zeroing ICR/MADR-style fields), a small helper called repeatedly with small integer arguments (`0xBFC4D370`, most likely a boot-progress/debug-print routine, called with `0xf`, `0xe`, `1`, `4`, `5`, `6`, ... in sequence - consistent with a numbered stage-tracking convention, distinct from the earlier `0xBF802070` progress-byte convention seen in the 120th/121st findings), and several more instances of the exact ROMDIR-catalog-scan-plus-conditional-jump pattern the 121st finding already documented (`0xBFC4EDA4`/`0xBFC58AD0`-style call pairs, reused here for what appear to be additional embedded images). In total the function's first ~400 instructions alone reference at least 30 distinct callee subroutines.

**A targeted static search for the simplest possible install mechanism came up empty.** Automated (Capstone) disassembly of the first ~1,000 instructions of each of these ~30 first-level callees, searching for any direct `sw`/`sh`/`sb <reg>, <imm>($zero)` instruction whose immediate falls in the exact target range (RAM `0x3F0`-`0x490`, covering the 119th finding's `0x400`-`0x47C` table plus its `0x40`-`0x74` context-save code), found **zero matches** across all 30 targets. This rules out - at this specific call-graph depth, for this specific mechanism - a trivial single-instruction store as the install method.

**Honest assessment of what this negative result does and doesn't mean.** It does NOT mean the install doesn't happen somewhere in this call graph - a real BIOS installing a fixed handler stub into RAM very plausibly does so via a register-relative copy loop (a moving pointer incremented each iteration, e.g. `lw $v0,0($t0); sw $v0,0($t1); addiu $t0,$t0,4; addiu $t1,$t1,4; bne ...`), which uses no compile-time-constant offset and is therefore invisible to this round's constant-offset grep. It also doesn't rule out the install living one or more calls deeper than this first level (a callee of a callee). Both remain open, and neither was chased further this round given the scope already covered.

**No live watchpoint attempt this round.** The existing live GT3 DebugServer session (used for the 119th finding) is already well past boot, paused mid-gameplay - a watchpoint set now on IOP RAM `0x400`-`0x47C` could not retroactively catch the original, one-time boot-writes that already happened before this session was ever connected to. The connected PCSX2 MCP toolset exposes pause/continue/breakpoints/watchpoints/read/disassemble but no reset/restart capability, so there is no way to re-trigger a genuine cold boot and catch the real write event live without the user manually restarting the game in PCSX2 itself - noted as a real, but not yet exercised, option for a future round.

**No fix this round - static analysis and host-native verification only.** `PRId` remains at its safe value of 0 in the shipped build; no source change, regression/rebuild skipped per standing convention for docs-only rounds.

**Concrete next step for task #245**: either (a) extend the static search to look for register-relative copy-loop patterns (backward branch plus an incrementing `lw`/`sw` pair) across the same ~30-subroutine call graph rather than constant-offset stores, or (b) if a future round has the opportunity, use a real hardware watchpoint on a freshly-restarted live GT3 session to catch the exact write event directly - the most reliable method, not yet attempted.

## 123rd finding (Round 83, task #245, task #172 continuation): live write-watchpoint on a real, user-triggered cold reset captures the exact post-install byte content of the real exception-vector table - confirms real semantics, rules out a verbatim ROM-to-RAM template copy, and identifies a real gap in this thread's own search methodology

Directly continuing the 122nd finding's flagged next step, using a genuinely live capture this time instead of further static analysis. Per the user's request, a write watchpoint was armed on the live GT3 DebugServer session (IOP RAM `0x40`-`0x480`, `action=break`) and the user then reset the game and kept the PCSX2 window focused themselves - avoiding the tool-side pause/continue friction that blocked earlier attempts this session. The watchpoint fired and produced a full register + memory report.

**The real exception-vector table's exact byte content is now on record.** The captured `0x40`-`0x47C` dump matches the 119th finding's structural description precisely and adds the concrete bytes: the context-save code at `0x40`-`0x74` (`sw k0,0x420(zero)` etc., byte-identical in shape to the earlier live disassembly), the general-exception vector at `0x80`-`0xB4`, and - new this round - the fully-populated 16-entry `Cause.ExcCode`-indexed jump table at `0x440`-`0x47C`. Decoding it entry-by-entry shows real, semantically-correct MIPS dispatch: `ExcCode=0` (Interrupt) gets its own handler (`0x00004B3C`), `ExcCode=8` (Syscall) gets its own handler (`0x00005038`), and all 14 other exception codes share one common/generic handler (`0x00003A68`) - exactly the shape a real kernel's exception dispatch table should have, and a level of semantic detail this project didn't have concrete evidence for before this capture.

**Searching the ROM binary for this exact byte sequence found no match - ruling out a simple verbatim memcpy install.** Neither the `0x40`-`0x74` code bytes nor the `0x440`-`0x47C` jump-table bytes appear anywhere in `/tmp/real_bios.bin` as a contiguous match. This rules out the simplest possible install mechanism (copying a pre-baked ROM template byte-for-byte into RAM) and is consistent with the jump-table values themselves being real, dynamically-relocated RAM addresses (e.g. `0x00003A68`, `0x00004B3C`, `0x00005038` - all low IOP-RAM addresses in the same general region as other kernel code this thread has already mapped, not ROM addresses) rather than static constants - i.e., the real kernel likely assembles this table at runtime from values it computes (handler addresses after its own relocation/loading), not from a static template.

**This retroactively identifies a real gap in the 122nd finding's own search methodology - an honest correction.** That round's automated scan only searched for direct `sw/sh/sb <reg>, <imm>(\`$zero\`)` instructions with the target address as a literal immediate. If the real install instead loads the destination address into an ordinary register first (e.g. `li $t0, 0x440`) and then stores through that register (`sw $reg, 0($t0)`, `sw $reg, 4($t0)`, ...), or uses a loop with a moving pointer, that scan would never have found it - and evidently didn't. This is recorded plainly as a real limitation of that round's technique, not a dead end for the underlying question.

**Practical, honest note on this round's live-capture method.** The watchpoint's reported "hit PC" landed on an unrelated tight self-loop at `0x0000B694` (a real, separate spin - likely a distinct polling wait elsewhere in the kernel's post-install runtime, not the install code itself), and the reported "accessed address" was not resolved by the tooling used to capture it. This means the exact instruction that performed the write is still not directly identified from this capture - but the resulting memory content is unambiguous, live, real, and byte-exact, which is a meaningfully stronger form of evidence than this thread has had for the table's contents until now.

**No source change this round.** `PRId` remains at its safe value of 0 in the shipped build; this was a live-capture and analysis round, regression/rebuild skipped per standing convention for docs-only rounds.

**Concrete next step for task #245**: re-run the Round 82-style automated search over the same ~30 kernel-main subroutine call graph, this time also matching register-relative store patterns (`sw <reg>, <small-offset>(<non-zero base register>)`) where the base register was recently set via `li`/`lui+ori` to a value in the `0x40`-`0x480` range - the corrected version of last round's search, informed directly by this round's ROM-search negative result.

## 124th finding (Round 84, task #245, task #172 continuation): corrected search confirms a real, shared "sparse RAM clear" subroutine at 0xBFC4D2A0 called directly from kernel-main - but it's a clear, not the install; broader search proved too noisy, and the 123rd finding's capture reveals a real watchpoint-granularity limitation

Directly continuing the 123rd finding's flagged next step (a register-relative store search, correcting the 122nd finding's `$zero`-only blind spot).

**Confirmed: `0xBFC4D2A0` is a real, callable low-RAM sparse-clear subroutine, called directly by kernel-main.** The corrected search (tracking simple `lui`+`ori`/`addiu` register loads before matching `sw`/`sh`/`sb <reg>, <offset>(<base>)` against the target range) found a clean, unambiguous hit: `$t2` is set to `0` a few instructions before a loop body that stores `$zero` to offsets `0x00,0x10,0x20,...,0x70` relative to `$t2`, incrementing `$t2` by `0x80` each iteration until it reaches `0xF80` - an exact structural match for the SAME sparse (8-of-32-words-per-block) RAM-clear pattern the 120th finding already documented as part of `0xBFC02000`'s own inline bring-up sequence. This is real, new information: it's not only inlined early in boot, it's also a genuine, separately-callable subroutine that this round's Round 82 call-graph shows kernel-main invokes directly (`jal 0xBFC4D2A0`). It clears the target region - it does not write the real handler content there.

**The broader search, run across kernel-main's own ~10,000-instruction body, produced too much noise to trust.** Extending the same register-tracking technique to kernel-main's full body (rather than just its first-level callees) returned 60 nominal "hits," but inspecting them shows the tracked "base register" values are implausibly small (`0x1`, `0x2e`, `0x51`, `0xa0`, ...) - clearly local variables, loop indices, or struct-field computations unrelated to any real RAM address, misidentified as address bases by this simple, control-flow-blind tracker. **This is an honest methodological ceiling, not a new lead**: a naive linear register tracker that doesn't model branches, calls (which clobber registers), or real dataflow cannot reliably answer this question at the scale of a real ~10,000-instruction kernel dispatcher. Chasing this further would need a proper dataflow-aware disassembler, which is out of scope for this investigative thread as currently tooled.

**A real, useful insight from re-examining the 123rd finding's capture in light of this round's result.** The 123rd finding's live watchpoint (armed on the full `0x40`-`0x480` write range) fired only once, yet its memory dump showed the COMPLETE, correctly-populated real table - not the freshly-zeroed state this round's confirmed clear routine would produce if the watchpoint had broken on ITS write (which, given the clear routine's real position in the boot sequence, would almost certainly execute before the real content install). This is a real, honestly-drawn inference, not a guess: PCSX2's DebugServer watchpoint implementation for the IOP likely checks at a coarser granularity than individual instructions (e.g., per recompiled block or per scheduler slice) - meaning by the time it actually paused execution, substantially more code had already run than just the one triggering write, including the entire real install. This means a narrower single-address watchpoint would very likely suffer the same imprecision, not just the wide range used - a genuine constraint on this investigative avenue worth recording plainly rather than silently re-attempting the same technique and hoping for a cleaner result.

**No fix this round - static analysis and methodological accounting only.** `PRId` remains at its safe value of 0 in the shipped build; no source change, regression/rebuild skipped per standing convention for docs-only rounds.

**Concrete next step for task #245**: given both the static (noisy, control-flow-blind) and live (coarse-grained watchpoint) approaches have now hit real, honestly-documented limitations, the most promising remaining avenue is a genuine PC-based code breakpoint (rather than a memory watchpoint) placed at specific candidate call sites within kernel-main's later call graph (calls this thread has not yet examined individually, beyond the first ~400 instructions Round 82 covered) - code breakpoints are typically exact even under JIT/recompiler execution, unlike memory watchpoints. This has not yet been attempted and would require another live session.

## 125th finding (Round 85, task #245, task #172 continuation): a second live capture, using a completely different watchpoint configuration, reproduces the prior capture byte-for-byte - conclusively demonstrating this debugger's watchpoint reports are not instruction-precise for this investigation, and closing out the live-watchpoint avenue

Directly following the 124th finding's watchpoint-granularity concern, this round tested it directly rather than leaving it as an inference: a second live capture was taken with a deliberately different watchpoint - narrowed from the 123rd finding's wide `0x40`-`0x480` write range down to a single 4-byte word (`0x440`-`0x444`), and changed from `write` to `onchange` type, on a fresh cold-boot GT3 session the user reset and kept focused themselves (same careful, tool-side-hands-off procedure as the 123rd finding).

**The result is byte-for-byte identical to the 123rd finding's capture in every respect**: hit PC (`0x0000B694`), every GPR (including `k0=0x0000B694`, `ra=0x0000C46C`, `gp=0x00019A50`, `sp=fp=0x001FEFE0`), and the entire `0x40`-`0x480` memory dump match exactly. The only difference between the two reports is a slightly wider disassembly window in this round's report (revealing one earlier instruction, `jal 0xC7D0` at `0x0000B658`, otherwise unchanged).

**This is a strong, reproducible result, not a coincidence, and it conclusively answers the 124th finding's open question.** Two genuinely different watchpoint configurations - different address range, different width (0x440 bytes vs. 4 bytes), different trigger type (`write` vs. `onchange`) - on two independent fresh cold boots, produced an identical stop point down to every register value. The only way this makes sense is if the reported "watchpoint hit" is not actually gated by the specific watchpoint's true trigger condition at all: this debugging setup most likely pauses at some fixed, deterministic point in time after boot (e.g., after a fixed delay, or at the next convenient scheduler/frame boundary) regardless of which watchpoint is configured, landing on whatever the IOP is doing at that moment - which happens to be a real, unrelated tight loop (`0x0000B694: j ->0x0000B694`) that the kernel settles into shortly after boot completes, not the actual instruction that installs the vector table.

**This closes out the live-watchpoint approach for this specific goal.** Since two structurally different watchpoint configurations produced an identical, non-informative result, a third attempt with yet another configuration (narrower range, different type, etc.) would very likely reproduce the same outcome again. The memory dump itself remains useful corroborating evidence (a second, independent confirmation of the real table's exact byte content, matching the 123rd finding precisely), but this technique cannot be relied on to pinpoint the exact writing instruction with the tooling available in this environment.

**No fix this round.** `PRId` remains at its safe value of 0 in the shipped build; no source change, regression/rebuild skipped per standing convention for docs-only rounds.

**Honest summary of task #245's overall state after this thread of investigation.** Across the 116th-125th findings, this project has: corrected a prior mischaracterization of the device-table dispatcher (116th); discovered and implemented real ELF-load handling for embedded device-table modules (117th); precisely isolated and diagnosed a real `$ra`-restoration bug in the resulting spin (118th); conclusively proven via live hardware comparison that the real exception-vector table is genuinely missing from this project's `PRId=0x1f` path (119th); traced the complete real boot chain from the raw reset vector through a PRId dispatch, RAM/cache bring-up, a ROMDIR-catalog scanner, and into the real kernel-main dispatcher (120th-122nd); captured the exact real byte content and semantics of the installed vector table twice, independently (123rd, 125th); and identified real, honest limits of both the static-analysis technique (control-flow-blind register tracking doesn't scale to a 10,000-instruction dispatcher) and the live-capture technique (this debugger's watchpoints are not instruction-precise here) available in this environment (124th, 125th). The exact instruction that performs the real install remains unidentified, but the surrounding mechanism, real content, and real semantics are now thoroughly documented and verified from multiple independent angles.

**Concrete next step for task #245, if pursued further**: true instruction-level precision would require single-instruction stepping (not watchpoints) from a known earlier point in the boot sequence - substantially more time-intensive than the approaches tried so far, and not attempted this round.

## 126th finding (Round 86, task #172 continuation): re-verified the 94th finding's splash-screen blocker on top of all intervening work - PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 are STILL never written; the interrupt/IOP-MMIO fixes did not resolve it, though more GS timing-config activity is now observed

This is consistent with, and adds concrete instrumented confirmation to, this project's own earlier informal observation (Round 77-era notes) that "GS privileged registers (SMODE1/SYNCH1/SYNCH2/SYNCV/SMODE2/SRFSH) show real-looking values" - the display's electrical/timing configuration is being set up for real, but the actual "what to show and where" registers never get touched.

## 127th finding (Round 87, task #172 continuation): implemented the real GS VSYNC interrupt and EE peripheral Timers T0-T3 (both previously completely unimplemented) - live evidence confirms real BIOS code now actively uses the new timers, but PMODE/DISPFB1/DISPLAY1 still aren't written because a stuck Status.EXL=1 blocks ALL interrupt delivery - a new, more fundamental blocker

Directly implementing the user's explicit request to "fix as much as possible so that the GS gets the writes" and to identify "what is missing to be implemented" - not another investigation-only round, but real source changes, tested and measured.

**Fix 1: real GS VSYNC interrupt (EE_INTC bit 0).** `gs.c`'s own header comment admits "we don't generate real GS interrupts yet," and `ee_intc.h` never defined a GS IRQ constant. Added `ee_check_gs_vsync()` in `ee_core.c`, gated on GS_IMR bit 3 (VSMSK, real CSR/IMR bit layout already documented in this project), raising EE_INTC source 0 once per real NTSC frame (same `EE_CYCLES_PER_FRAME_NTSC` constant `ee_check_vblank()` already uses). Wired into both existing per-instruction step call sites, matching `ee_check_vblank()`'s placement exactly. Verified via a scratch-copy diagnostic hook: the interrupt genuinely fires (162 times over a 100M-instruction run) with GS_IMR unmasked. **Result: zero change to the GS-write diagnostic** - not because the fix is wrong, but because `INTC_MASK` at rest is `0x00001002` (only SBUS and TIMER3 unmasked) - real software isn't listening for GS or VBLANK at this point at all. A real, correct, now-implemented gap, but not what's blocking progress right now.

**Fix 2: real EE peripheral Timers T0-T3 (`include/core/hw/ee_timers.h`, `source/hw/ee_timers.c`) - previously completely unimplemented.** Confirmed via grep (zero hits) and via `ee_mem_read32`/`write32`'s own pre-existing comment in `ee_core.c`, which explicitly names "timers" among the addresses that "still fall through to the silent-no-op ... path." This is a real, distinct piece of EE hardware from the already-implemented COP0 Count/Compare mechanism (real addresses `0x10000000`/`+0x800`/`+0x1000`/`+0x1800` for T0-T3, each with COUNT/MODE/COMP, T0/T1 additionally with HOLD - per PCSX2's `Hw.h` EERegisterAddresses). Modeled following this project's established "1 instruction = 1 cycle" simplification and the same honestly-scoped-down approach already used for `iop_timers.c` (real CUE/CMPE/OVFE/REPEAT_IRQ/EQUF/OVFF bit semantics ported directly; CLKS alternate clock sources, gate modes, and HOLD's real external-signal latching explicitly NOT modeled). Wired into `ee_core.c`'s MMIO dispatch (`ee_mem_read32`/`write32`, alongside the existing `dma_mmio_.../sif_mmio_.../ee_intc_mmio_...` checks) and into the per-instruction step epilogue (`ee_timers_tick()`, both call sites, same placement as `ee_check_vblank()`/`ee_check_gs_vsync()`).

**Live evidence real BIOS code immediately starts using the new timers.** A scratch-copy diagnostic hook on `ee_timers_mmio_write32()` shows real code writing all 4 timers' MODE/COUNT/COMP/HOLD registers early in the run: T0 and T1 get `MODE=CUE` only (plain free-running counters, no IRQ), while **T2 and T3 get `MODE=CUE|OVFE`** (overflow interrupt explicitly enabled) - and all four timers' COMP register is set to exactly `0x0000FFFF`.

**Caught and fixed a real bug before it mattered: EE timer counters are 16-bit, not 32-bit.** The first draft of `ee_timers_tick()` modeled COUNT as a full 32-bit free-running counter (reasoning: unlike the IOP's T0-T2/T3-T5 split, nothing in this project had previously established EE counter width). The live evidence above is the tell: `COMP=0xFFFF` on *all four* timers is the exact maximum value of a 16-bit counter, not a coincidental 32-bit constant - real code is arming these timers to fire on natural 16-bit wraparound, matching real PS2 EE hardware (T0-T3 are genuinely 16-bit, unlike the IOP's mixed-width block). With the original 32-bit model, this timer would have taken ~4.3 billion ticks to overflow instead of 65536 - meaning the real "wants an overflow interrupt roughly every 65536 EE cycles" behavior would have silently never fired within any realistic diagnostic run. Fixed `ee_timers_tick()` to wrap at `0xFFFF`, matching the IOP's own `max_count=0xFFFFu` treatment of its 16-bit timers (T0-T2) in `iop_timers.c`.

**Re-tested after the fix: T2 and T3's overflow interrupts now genuinely fire and reach INTC_STAT.** A final-state diagnostic dump after a 100M-instruction run shows `T2.mode=0x1c00` and `T3.mode=0x1c03` - both missing their original OVFE bit (`0x80`), meaning each fired its one-shot overflow interrupt and (correctly, matching the real "one-shot disables further IRQs until MODE is rewritten" semantics already established for the IOP model) auto-disabled OVFE afterward, having done so at least once. `INTC_STAT=0x0000180d` confirms both TIMER2 (bit 11) and TIMER3 (bit 12) are set pending, alongside GS/VBLANK_S/VBLANK_E (bits 0/2/3, from the vsync fix and pre-existing VBLANK model). `INTC_MASK=0x00001002` unmasks TIMER3 specifically - so `ee_intc_pending()` now correctly reports 1 (a real IP2 interrupt source is pending AND unmasked) for the first time in this project's history.

**New, more fundamental discovery: `Status.EXL=1` is permanently stuck, blocking ALL interrupt delivery regardless of source.** Despite `ee_intc_pending()` now correctly returning 1, `Cause.IP2` (`0x400`) never gets set - only `Cause.IP7` (`0x8000`, the pre-existing COP0 Timer/Compare line) is present at rest. The reason is structural: `ee_check_intc_interrupt()` (and `ee_check_dmac_interrupt()`) both gate on `(Status & (IE|EXL|ERL|EIE)) == (IE|EIE)` - i.e. they refuse to fire if `EXL` is set, which is correct real MIPS behavior (a CPU already inside exception-handling context shouldn't take nested exceptions) but means that if `EXL` never gets cleared, no new interrupt - old or new - can ever be delivered. A final-state register dump shows `Status=0x70030c13` (`IE=1, EXL=1, ERL=0, EIE=1`) at rest. This is not caused by this round's changes: the EE's resting PC (`0x80005E5C`) is identical to the 94th/122nd/126th findings' measurements, all taken before this round's fixes existed - this is a pre-existing condition, newly explained rather than newly introduced.

**Disassembled the resting PC to understand what's actually happening.** `0x80005E5C` (`lui v0,0xb000` / `ori v0,v0,0xf230` / `lw a0,0(v0)`) is a plain busy-wait: real code repeatedly reads a fixed low-memory location (physical `0x0000F230`, well below the `0x10000000` hardware-register window - an ordinary RAM address, not a peripheral) and, per the immediately preceding subroutine (`lw v0,(v1); bnel a0,v0,-88; ...; jr ra`), loops until it changes. Nothing in this emulation currently writes to that address, so real code is durably parked here regardless of what interrupts reach `Cause.IP2` - explaining why even a correctly-pending, correctly-unmasked TIMER3 interrupt makes no observable difference to the GS-write diagnostic: the interrupt is pending but architecturally un-deliverable while `EXL` stays stuck, and even if it could be delivered, the code waiting at `0x80005E5C` isn't obviously the code that would act on it.

**Full regression suite (90/90 tests) and a clean Wii/devkitPPC rebuild both pass** with these changes in place - no other test's behavior changed.

**Concrete next step for task #172**: the real blocker has shifted from "no interrupt sources exist" (true before this round) to "an interrupt source now exists, is correctly pending and unmasked, but `Status.EXL` never gets cleared to allow delivery." The next productive step is tracing why `EXL` gets set and never cleared via `ERET` (which this project already implements, per `ee_core.c` funct `0x18`) - either a real exception handler this project reaches never calls `ERET` (a genuine emulation gap), or real code intentionally holds `EXL=1` across an extended real critical section that this project's boot never properly exits. A second, parallel thread worth tracing: what real mechanism is meant to write physical `0x0000F230` (the value `0x80005E5C`'s busy-wait is reading) - if that's a distinct, addressable gap (e.g., a specific SIF/RPC reply or interrupt-handler side effect this project doesn't yet produce), unblocking it directly could resolve the busy-wait independent of the EXL question.

## 128th finding (Round 88, task #172/#247 continuation): corrected the 127th finding's framing - Status.EXL=1 is genuine, deliberate real PS2 kernel bootstrap behavior (a directly-loaded constant), not a stuck/leaked exception; the real remaining blocker is still the busy-wait on physical 0x0000F230

Directly following up on task #247 (filed at the end of Round 87 to investigate why Status.EXL never clears). Host-native instrumentation (scratch copies only, `/tmp/pcsx2-instrument12`, real repo untouched this round) traced every call to `ee_raise_exception()` and every `MTC0`-to-Status write across a 30M-instruction run.

**Zero exceptions were ever raised via `ee_raise_exception()` in this run - the exception-delivery path was never even entered.** This immediately ruled out the 127th finding's working theory ("the EE is inside an unresolved exception handler that never calls ERET"): there's no handler to be stuck inside, because no exception was ever taken in the first place.

**Traced every direct write to Status (COP0 register 12) instead - exactly two, in the entire run.** The first (`pc=0xBFC00814, val=0x70400000`) is early ROM boot code, already covered by this project's prior work. The second (`pc=0x80001050, val=0x70030c13`) is the one that leaves `EXL=1` - and disassembling the surrounding code shows this is unmistakably real, deliberate kernel bootstrap code, not a bug: `lui v0,0x8001` / `lw v0,0x2484(v0)` loads a fixed 32-bit constant from a kernel data table at `0x80012484`, then `mtc0 v0,$12` writes it directly to Status, followed by a `SYNC` (memory barrier), then the identical pattern for `Config` (constant from `0x80012488` into COP0 register 16 via `mtc0 v0,$16`), another `SYNC`, then a `jal` into a further subroutine (`0x8000c0b8`). This is a real, well-formed "load canonical Status/Config from a static table" pattern - exactly what a real kernel's own early bootstrap does, not a mistake or garbage value.

**This means the 127th finding's framing was wrong, and this round corrects it plainly.** `Status.EXL=1` is not "stuck" or "leaked" - it's the genuine, intended value real PS2 kernel code sets at this exact point in boot, matching what this project's disassembly independently confirms. Recorded as an honest correction rather than silently revised.

**The real open question this reframes, rather than closes, task #247**: given real PCSX2's own cited interrupt-gating logic (`cpuTestTIMRInts()`/`cpuTestINTCInts()`, already ported into this project's `ee_check_timer_interrupt()`/`ee_check_intc_interrupt()`/`ee_check_dmac_interrupt()`) requires `EXL=0` to take ANY interrupt, and real kernel code apparently sets `EXL=1` this early and (in this project's current boot) never clears it again, the real mechanism must be that later, further-downstream real kernel code eventually clears `EXL` again (via `ERET` or another direct Status write) - this project's boot just hasn't reached that point. The call chain leading up to the Status write (`0x80001028`: `jal 0x80005B90`; `0x80001030`: `jal 0x80002050`; `0x80001038`: `jal 0x8000AE88`; `0x80001040`: `jal 0x80004EC8`; then the Status/Config load; then `0x8000106c`: `jal 0x8000C0B8`) all complete and return normally in this run - meaning the busy-wait this project's boot gets stuck at (`~0x80005E5C-0x80005E60`, close to but distinct from the first subroutine's own entry point `0x80005B90`) is reached from somewhere further downstream of `0x8000C0B8`, not from getting permanently stuck inside any of these four early calls. Whatever clears `EXL` on real hardware almost certainly lives further down that same call chain, past the point this project's boot currently stalls.

## 129th finding (Round 89, task #172/#247 continuation): pinpointed the exact busy-wait mechanism and its full request/poll protocol - a software-internal async request pattern this project's single-threaded EE model has no way to service; declined to fake the completion flag

Directly continuing from the 128th finding's corrected framing and its flagged next step: tracing forward from `jal 0x8000C0B8` (called right after the real Status/Config bootstrap load) to find where the busy-wait at `~0x80005E5C` is actually reached from.

**Traced the exact call path via host-native PC-coverage instrumentation** (scratch copy `/tmp/pcsx2-instrument13`, real repo untouched). A ring-buffer of the last 4000 executed PCs, dumped the instant the busy-wait is first reached (`step 29930488` of a 35M-instruction run), shows: `0x8000C0B8` returns normally to `0x80001074`, which `jal`s into `0x80006198` - a real function containing two short, legitimate, bounded polling loops (7 and 15 iterations respectively - these complete, they are not the blocker) before calling two setup subroutines and finally `jal 0x80005E58` in a tight loop.

**Disassembled the full protocol.** `0x80006308` (called at `0x8000625C`) builds what has the exact bit layout of a real EE DMA chain tag (`0x20000000` = `QWC=0, ID=2/CNT` in the real DMAtag format used throughout this project's own `dma.c`) at a fixed kernel-RAM struct (`0x8001E330`/`+4`), writes a status byte (`0x1E`) and a halfword (`0xFFFF`) to another fixed location (`0x8001E104`/`0x8001E106`), and separately writes the physical address of that struct (`0x0001E140`) to a small kernel mailbox at physical `0x0000C430` (clearing `0x0000C420` first). Then `0x80006AE8` (a tiny real accessor: write-then-read-back) is called with `a0=0`, writing `0` to physical `0x0000F200`. Finally, `jal 0x80005E58` is called in a loop (`0x80006268`-`0x80006274`): `0x80005E58` reads a 32-bit value from physical `0x0000F230` and returns it; the caller `AND`s the result with `0x00010000` and loops back if that bit is still 0.

**Verified this is NOT a hardware-register gap - it's genuine, unbacked kernel-internal RAM, confirmed by direct comparison against this project's own real DMA channel address table.** `dma.c`'s own `DMAC_BASE=0x10008000` and its full per-channel table (`VIF0=0x10008000`, `VIF1=0x10009000`, etc.) are the real EE hardware DMA registers - none within a factor of `0x10000000` of the `0x0000C400-0x0000C440` and `0x0000F200-0x0000F260` addresses this protocol actually touches. A grep across every hardware model file in this project (`dma.c`, `sif.c`, `gs.c`, `ee_intc.c`, `ee_timers.c`, `mch.c`) for any of these specific addresses returns zero hits. This rules out the otherwise-natural hypothesis that this is simply a not-yet-wired MMIO register (the pattern this project has fixed many times before, e.g. the 127th finding's EE Timers). These reads/writes already work correctly as ordinary RAM in this project - there is no missing dispatch case to add.

**This is a real, software-internal asynchronous request/completion pattern - and this project's EE model has no mechanism to service the "async" half of it.** The shape (build a descriptor, write a request-ready flag, poll a completion flag) is a textbook kernel primitive for "hand this off to something else, then wait for it to finish" - real PS2 kernels commonly implement this via genuine concurrent thread scheduling (the requesting code blocks/polls while a *different* schedulable context - another thread, or a real interrupt handler - performs the work and posts completion). This project's EE core executes one single, flat, linear instruction stream with no concept of a second concurrent execution context or a real thread scheduler - unlike the IOP side of this project, which already has exactly this kind of infrastructure (task #238's "persistent IOP idle/scheduler loop"). The EE side has no equivalent.

**Deliberately did not implement a fix that writes the completion bit directly.** Setting physical `0x0000F230` bit 16 to `1` from outside this exact protocol would make the busy-wait exit, but it would be an unprincipled hack with no real-hardware justification behind it - this project's entire fix history (every finding from the 1st through the 128th) has been citation-backed and semantically grounded in real hardware/kernel behavior, never a bypass chosen just to unblock a diagnostic. Faking this flag risks leaving the DMA-tag-shaped descriptor at `0x8001E330` half-processed (nothing would actually consume it), and risks masking whatever the real next blocker turns out to be behind a false "success" signal. This is recorded as a deliberate choice, not an oversight.

**No source change this round - instrumentation and disassembly only, real repo untouched.** Regression/rebuild skipped per standing convention for docs-only rounds.

**Concrete next step for task #247**: the honest options are (a) determine what real subsystem/interrupt is meant to consume the DMA-tag-shaped descriptor at `0x8001E330` and post the real completion signal - would need identifying the real kernel function this maps to (candidates: a real GS-packet-send primitive, given the timing relative to the already-observed SMODE/SYNCH GS register writes; or a real semaphore/thread-signal primitive, given the `0x1E`/`0xFFFF` status-field pattern resembles thread/semaphore state), most likely via a fresh live PCSX2 comparison targeting this exact address range and call site; or (b) scope out and implement genuine EE-side concurrent scheduling infrastructure (the EE-side equivalent of task #238's IOP scheduler) if the real blocker turns out to be architectural rather than a single missing peripheral. Given the address range's DMA-tag shape and its temporal proximity to the already-confirmed GS timing-register writes (126th finding), option (a) targeting a GS-related kernel primitive is the more promising lead to try first.
